title: How Propaganda Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss propaganda: its classical definition as persuasive argument that selectively omits facts, a brief history starting with the Catholic Congregation of Propaganda (1622), and the common techniques named in the article: name calling, bandwagon, glittering generalities, card stacking, testimonials-style transfer, subliminal imagery, and plain folks. They cover how bias creeps into journalism, the Internet as both undermining and spreading propaganda, religious and government propaganda (including the 2005 Stop Government Propaganda Now Act), Nazi propaganda and WWII American posters like Rosie the Riveter, and how propaganda shaped women's and minorities' roles. The episode closes with listener mail correcting the gender of Mollie Orshansky, creator of the poverty line.

entities.name: Stuff You Missed in History Class

segments.title: Opening banter and Cold War memories
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with chat about Chuck's night out at Matt's band and then reminisce about growing up during the Cold War and anti-Soviet propaganda in movies.

segments.title: Defining propaganda
segments.summary: The hosts define propaganda in its classical sense as persuasive arguments that use facts but omit facts that would favor the other side, and note the word's negative connotations. They discuss anti-smoking ads as an example.

segments.title: History of the word propaganda
segments.summary: The hosts trace the word to the Catholic Congregation of Propaganda established by Pope Gregory XV in 1622 to win back Catholics drawn to Protestantism after Martin Luther.

segments.title: Ethics of propaganda and Emlyn Brunner
segments.summary: Chuck discusses professor Emlyn Brunner's view that good propaganda depends on whether its makers have the audience's best interests at heart. Josh disagrees, arguing that propaganda omits facts so no one is fully informed.

segments.title: Name calling, bandwagon, and glittering generalities
segments.summary: The hosts describe name calling (with examples of political labels), the bandwagon technique of getting on the winning side, and glittering generalities using positive words like liberty and family, illustrated with the Patriot Act.

segments.title: Card stacking and fear propaganda
segments.summary: Card stacking is described as stacking an argument by omitting negatives, with an Ali G example about Jim Broadwater. The hosts then discuss a joking name-calling example about Tech Stuff hosts and political fear ads such as the phone-ringing 3 a.m. commercial.

segments.title: Subliminal messaging, transfer, and plain folks
segments.summary: The hosts explain subliminal imagery in campaign posters such as red, white and blue and waving flags, the transfer technique and imagining oneself from another country, and plain folks propaganda with the example of a candidate fishing.

segments.title: Media, bias, and the Internet
segments.summary: The hosts discuss propaganda in movies and Rambo and Rocky, broadcast media as most dangerous because it's one-sided, news bias through journalistic choices, and how the Internet can both undermine and spread propaganda; Snopes is recommended.

segments.title: Types of propaganda: religious, thought reform, government
segments.summary: The hosts cover religious propaganda and missionaries, thought reform, the divisive us-versus-them effect, and government propaganda, including the 2005 Stop Government Propaganda Now Act signed by Bush.

segments.title: Nazi, WWII, and American wartime propaganda
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Nazi radio and films, WWII American posters including Uncle Sam and Rosie the Riveter, a poster comparing carpooling to riding with Hitler, and how wartime propaganda helped expand women's and black workers' roles.

segments.title: Listener mail: Mollie Orshansky's gender
segments.summary: A listener notes that Mollie Orshansky, who developed the poverty line, is a woman, not a man as the hosts had said. Josh and Chuck acknowledge the error and share her background at the Social Security Administration.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners for email and direct them to the website and blog.
